usage: to take out of a bag
에서 (out of) marks the enclosed space; this is the bread-and-butter pattern for 꺼내다
the figurative sense: literally 'pull a story out' — said when someone raises a sensitive subject
withdrawing cash or pulling bills from a wallet — note 인출하다 is the bank/ATM word, 꺼내다 is the hand action
the helper-verb 주다 makes it a favor: 'get it out for me' from a high shelf or deep bag
examples: 가방에서 지갑 꺼내.
Take your wallet out of the bag.
casual command to a close friend; bare stem 꺼내 is the plainest form
냉장고에서 반찬 좀 꺼내 줄래?
Can you take the side dishes out of the fridge?
줄래? is the soft favor-asking you use with a roommate or partner
친구가 갑자기 그 얘기를 꺼내서 좀 놀랐어요.
My friend suddenly brought up that topic, so I was a bit startled.
real-situation figurative use: 얘기를 꺼내다 = raise/bring up a topic; 갑자기 (suddenly) sharpens the surprise
nuance: 꺼내다 is the default verb for taking something out of an enclosed space — a bag, pocket, fridge, drawer — so it almost always pairs with 에서 marking the place. The nearest rival is 빼다: the dividing line is that 빼다 is pulling out something fitted or stuck (a key from a lock, a tooth, a USB), while 꺼내다 is retrieving a freely-resting thing from inside. It's a plain native verb with no 한자, and the 내- piece carries an 'outward' feel (compare 내보내다 'send out'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 빼다 because 'take out' feels like 'pull out'; the second pitfall is the figurative 얘기를 꺼내다 ('bring up a topic') — learners try 가져오다 ('bring') here, but Korean specifically 'pulls the words out,' so 꺼내다 is required.

Saying 얘기를 가져오다 to mean 'bring up a topic' — 가져오다 is physically fetching an object. To raise a subject you 'pull it out': 그 얘기 왜 꺼냈어? (Why did you bring that up?).
Forgetting the 에서 and using 에 — it is 가방에서 꺼내다 (out of), not 가방에 꺼내다; 에 would point to a destination, the wrong direction for 'taking out.'

usage: (으)로 marks the tool; the prototypical 집다 scene is grasping food with chopsticks
to pick up and hand over
집어 주세요 = pick it up and give it to me, the everyday 'hand me that' favor
집다 + 들다 = grab and lift in one motion, e.g. casually taking a product off a store shelf
selecting a single small item from several — a candy, a card, one piece
examples: 그거 좀 집어 줘.
Pick that up for me.
bare casual request; 집어 줘 is what you say when your hands are full
고기 집을 집게 좀 주세요.
Can I get tongs to pick up the meat?
everyday Korean BBQ line; note 집게 (tongs) literally is 'the picking-up tool' from 집다
마트에서 아무거나 집지 말고 유통기한부터 확인해.
At the store, don't just grab whatever — check the expiration date first.
real-situation 집다 = casually grabbing an item off a shelf, here in a negative -지 말다 command
nuance: 집다 means to pick up a small object with a precise pincer grasp — fingers, chopsticks, or tongs (집게, literally 'the picking tool,' comes straight from this verb). The contrast learners need is with 들다 (to lift/raise with the hand or arm) and 줍다 (to pick up off the ground something dropped): you 집어 a single fry, 들어 a heavy box, and 주워 a coin that fell. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The single biggest pitfall is conjugation: because it ends in ㅂ, English speakers over-apply the ㅂ-irregular and write 지워요, but 집다 is REGULAR — like its cousins 잡다 and 좁다 it keeps the ㅂ, so the 요-form is 집어요. A second trap is using 집다 for picking up off the floor; that situation wants 줍다.

Using 집다 for picking trash up off the ground — that is 줍다 (쓰레기를 줍다). 집다 is a controlled fingertip grasp, not retrieving something that fell.
Confusing 집다 with 들다 for heavy or large things — you 집어 a coin but you must 들어 (lift) a suitcase; 집다 only works on small graspable objects.

usage: set it down and come away — 핸드폰 두고 왔어요 'I left my phone behind' is daily-essential
그냥 둬 = leave it alone, don't touch it; the most common everyday phrase with 두다
to do in advance / keep done
auxiliary use: 사 두다 'buy and keep,' 해 두다 'get it done ahead' — preparing for later
the standard delivery instruction: set the package down and leave it there
examples: 여기 둬.
Put it here.
shortest casual form; note 두다 + 어 contracts the ㅜ to 둬, not 두요
우산 여기 뒀는데 어디 갔지?
I put my umbrella here, where did it go?
past 뒀어요 contracts from 두었어요; said when you can't find what you set down
지갑을 집에 두고 나와서 다시 들어갔어요.
I left my wallet at home, so I went back in.
real-situation 두고 나오다 = leave behind by accident, one of the most useful expressions for residents
nuance: 두다 means to place something somewhere and leave it resting there — the emphasis falls on the resulting stationary state, not the motion of setting it down. That is exactly how it splits from 놓다, its nearest synonym: 놓다 stresses the physical act of letting go onto a surface, whereas 두다 stresses leaving it (and often abandoning or keeping it) in place. It is also hugely productive as an auxiliary, -어 두다 meaning 'do something and keep it that way' (예약해 뒀어요 'I went ahead and booked it'). It's a plain native verb with no 한자. The grammar pitfall: 두다 is a ㅜ-stem, so 두 + 어요 contracts to 둬요 — English speakers often write the wrong 두요. The usage pitfall is reaching for 놓다 or 넣다 in 'I left it at home' sentences, where Korean firmly uses 두고 오다/나오다.

mistakes: Writing the polite form as 두요 — the ㅜ + 어 contraction is obligatory, so it must be 둬요 (or the full 두어요). The past is likewise 뒀어요, not 두었어요 in speech.
Saying 집에 놓고 왔어요 vs 두고 왔어요 carelessly — while 놓고 오다 exists, the idiomatic 'left it behind' that residents need is 두고 오다/나오다 (핸드폰 두고 왔어요).
Using 넣다 ('put in') when you mean leave-on-a-surface — 넣다 requires an inside (가방에 넣다). To leave a package at the door it is 문 앞에 두다, not 넣다.

usage: 에 marks the container; plating food into serving dishes is the core scene
the fixed online-shopping phrase — every Korean shopping app's button says 담기
checkout situation: 따로 담아 주세요 'please bag it separately'
to put one's heart into it
figurative: 정성을 담다 / 마음을 담아 — pour feeling into a gift, letter, or cooking
examples: 여기 좀 담아 줘.
Put some in here for me.
casual; 담아 from 담 + 아요, a regular ㅏ-friendly stem
장바구니에 담아 두고 나중에 결제했어요.
I added it to the cart and paid later.
everyday e-commerce: 장바구니에 담다 = add to cart, with -어 두다 'keep it there'
남은 음식은 반찬통에 담아서 냉장고에 넣으세요.
Put the leftovers in a container and into the fridge.
real kitchen instruction; notice 담다 fills the container, then 넣다 inserts it into the fridge
nuance: 담다 specifically means to load contents into a container — a bowl, box, bag, or shopping cart — so the focus is the container getting filled. Its nearest neighbor is 넣다 ('put in / insert'), and the line is clear: 넣다 emphasizes the inserting motion of one object into an opening (열쇠를 주머니에 넣다), while 담다 emphasizes filling a vessel with stuff, especially food or groceries. That is why every Korean shopping app labels its cart button 담기, and why plating is 그릇에 담다. It also has a warm figurative life — 마음을 담다 'put your heart in,' 정성을 담다 — which 넣다 cannot carry. It's a plain native verb, conjugating regularly (담 + 아요 = 담아요). Pitfall: English speakers default to 넣다 for bagging takeout, but natives say 봉투에 담아 주세요.

Saying 장바구니에 넣다 for 'add to cart' — the locked phrase online is 장바구니에 담다 (the button literally reads 담기). 넣다 sounds off here.
Trying 마음을 넣다 for 'put my heart into it' — the idiom is 마음을 담다 / 마음을 담아; 넣다 is too physical and is wrong for emotion or sincerity.

usage: spreading a book open to a page — the classic classroom command
spreading a floor mattress/blanket to sleep, a daily Korean-home action; its opposite is 이불을 개다 'fold up'
펴다 also un-bends a body part: 허리 좀 펴 = sit/stand up straight
popping an umbrella open; the reverse is 우산을 접다 'fold the umbrella'
examples: 손 펴 봐.
Open your hand.
simple casual command; bare stem 펴, here with 보다 'try and see'
교과서 30쪽 펴세요.
Open your textbook to page 30.
everyday teacher line; 책을 펴다 = open/spread a book
구겨진 영수증을 폈는데도 글씨가 안 보였어요.
Even after I flattened the crumpled receipt, I couldn't read it.
real-situation; note the past 폈어요 contracts from 펴 + 었어요
nuance: 펴다 is the all-purpose verb for unfolding, spreading out, or straightening — opening a book, laying out bedding, popping an umbrella, or un-bending your back. It is the direct everyday opposite of 접다 (to fold), and that pairing is the easiest way to fix its meaning. Learners often confuse it with 펼치다, which is showier and more spatial ('to unfurl, spread wide, roll out a plan/map'): you 펴 a single newspaper at the table but 펼쳐 a huge map across the floor or 꿈을 펼치다 'pursue a dream.' It's a plain native verb with no 한자. The reliable pitfall is the past tense: the ㅕ + 었 ALWAYS contracts, so it is 폈어요, never the spelled-out 펴었어요 — English speakers who reason form-by-form tend to leave it uncontracted.

mistakes: Writing the past tense as 펴었어요 — the ㅕ + 었 contracts obligatorily to 폈어요. Leaving it uncontracted is ungrammatical.
Using 펼치다 for ordinary unfolding — 책 폈어요 (opened the book), not 책 펼쳤어요 for the routine act. 펼치다 is for wide, dramatic spreading (지도를 펼치다, 날개를 펼치다).
Reaching for 열다 ('open') for an umbrella or bedding — 열다 is for doors, lids, and containers. An umbrella is 우산을 펴다 and bedding is 이불을 펴다, never 열다.

usage: the must-know phone-setup phrase in Korea — slot the SIM snugly in
wedging a thin thing into a gap between pages
fitting a ring onto a finger; the shorter 끼다 (반지를 끼다) is equally common
inserting something into a narrow gap — a note between pages, cheese between bread
examples: 여기 끼워.
Slot it in here.
bare casual; 끼우 + 어 contracts the ㅜ to 끼워
유심을 여기에 끼우면 돼요.
You just insert the SIM card here.
everyday phone-setup line residents hear constantly; 에 marks the slot
문에 발 끼우지 마세요, 다쳐요.
Don't get your foot caught in the door, you'll get hurt.
real-situation; 끼우다 also covers a body part getting wedged in a gap, here in negative -지 마세요
nuance: 끼우다 means to insert or wedge something snugly into a slot or gap so that it fits tightly — a SIM card into a tray, a cable into a port, a bookmark between pages, a ring onto a finger. The tight, fitted feel is exactly what separates it from 넣다 (loosely 'put in') and 담다 (fill a container): you 넣어 coins loosely into a piggy bank but 끼워 a SIM that has to click into place. Its plain twin 끼다 is just as natural for wearable fits (안경을 끼다 'wear glasses,' 장갑을 끼다 'wear gloves'). It's a native verb, no 한자, and as a ㅜ-stem it contracts 끼우 + 어 = 끼워요. Pitfall: English speakers say 유심을 넣다 because 'insert' feels generic, but a fitted insertion calls for 끼우다.

Forgetting the ㅜ + 어 contraction — the 요-form is 끼워요, not 끼우어요 spelled out; the past is 끼웠어요.
Confusing 끼우다 (you insert it) with the intransitive 끼다 in its 'get stuck' sense — note 끼다 can mean 'be wedged/stuck' on its own (문틈에 끼다), whereas 끼우다 is always you actively wedging something in.

usage: almost always pairs with 위에; the whole meaning is 'rest it on the upper surface'
to eat with (a topping) on top
food-hack phrasing: 라면에 치즈 얹어 먹다 'eat ramen with cheese on top'
어깨에 손을 얹다 'lay a hand on the shoulder' — a gentle, light placing
to set on top and leave
얹다 + 놓다 = rest it up there and leave it (선반에 얹어 놓다)
examples: 밥에 김 얹어.
Put some seaweed on the rice.
casual; 얹 + 어 = 얹어, keeping the ㅈ in spelling
라면에 치즈 한 장 얹어 먹어 봐.
Try eating your ramen with a slice of cheese on top.
everyday food-hack line; 얹어 먹다 = add a topping and eat
케이크 위에 딸기를 예쁘게 얹어 주세요.
Please arrange the strawberries nicely on top of the cake.
real bakery request; note 위에 marks the surface and 얹다 is the gentle placing of a topping
nuance: 얹다 means to rest or lay something lightly on top of a surface — an egg on rice, a hand on a shoulder, a strawberry on a cake — so it pairs almost reflexively with 위에 ('on top of'). It is gentler and far more specific than its neighbors 놓다 (general 'set down anywhere') and 두다 (leave somewhere): 놓다 just releases an object onto a surface, but 얹다 specifically frames it as perched on top of something else, often delicately. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The signature pitfall is spelling, because of the ㄵ cluster: when you add a vowel the sound resyllabifies to [언저], so learners wrongly write 언어요 — but the ㅈ must stay, giving 얹어요, 얹었어요, 얹어 주세요. A second trap is dropping 위에 and using a bare 에, which loses the 'on top' meaning.

mistakes: Spelling the 요-form as 언어요 — the ㄵ cluster is pronounced [언저] but written with the ㅈ intact: 얹어요, 얹었어요. Losing the ㅈ is a spelling error.
Using 놓다 when you mean 'rest on top of' — 놓다 only says you set it down somewhere; for perching one thing atop another you want 위에 얹다 (밥 위에 계란을 얹다).
Dropping 위에 and saying just 밥에 얹다 — the 'on top' nuance lives in 위에, so natural Korean keeps 밥 위에 얹다.

usage: (으)로 marks what you wrap around — towel, blanket, bubble wrap
담요로 몸을 감싸다 'wrap yourself in a blanket' for warmth or protection
both literal (cozily wrap) and figurative (defend a person): 나를 감싸 주다
enveloping something — a warm mug, someone's face — between both hands
examples: 수건으로 감싸.
Wrap it in a towel.
casual; 감싸 + 아 contracts fully so the stem already ends in the form you say
깨지지 않게 그릇을 뽁뽁이로 감싸 주세요.
Please wrap the dishes in bubble wrap so they don't break.
everyday shipping line; 뽁뽁이 = bubble wrap, 감싸다 = envelop to protect
다들 그 사람 욕할 때 친구만 나를 감싸 줬어요.
When everyone was bad-mouthing me, only my friend stood up for me.
real-situation figurative use; note you 감싸다 the person directly (나를), not 편을
nuance: 감싸다 means to wrap something around an object so as to cover, cushion, or protect it — a towel around wet hair, bubble wrap around dishes, a blanket around your shivering body — and it carries a distinct flavor of enveloping and shielding. That protective nuance is what separates it from the plain 싸다 ('wrap/pack,' as in wrapping a gift or packing a lunch): the 감- prefix (from 감다 'wind/coil around') adds the 'all the way around, enveloping' feeling. Figuratively it means to stand up for or shield a person — 나를 감싸 줬어요. It's a native verb (no 한자), a regular ㅏ-stem, so 감싸 + 았어요 contracts to 감쌌어요. Key pitfall: for 'take someone's side' English speakers invent 편을 감싸다, but you 감싸다 the person directly, while 'take a side' is the separate idiom 편을 들다.

Writing the past tense as 감싸았어요 — the ㅏ + 았 contracts fully to 감쌌어요.
Using the bare 싸다 when you mean protectively envelop — 싸다 is plain wrapping/packing (선물을 싸다, 도시락을 싸다); the 'wrap all around to protect' sense needs 감싸다.

usage: ripping open a snack bag or packet — the everyday core scene
tearing into a delivery box; 박스를 뜯다 likewise
opening mail/a bill to see inside: 고지서를 뜯어 보다
peeling a protective film off a new phone or screen
examples: 이거 좀 뜯어 줘.
Tear this open for me.
casual favor; 뜯 + 어 = 뜯어, a regular stem
과자 봉지 좀 뜯어 줄래?
Can you tear open the snack bag?
everyday request; 봉지를 뜯다 = rip open a bag, with soft -어 줄래?
포장 뜯지 말고 그대로 반품하세요.
Don't tear open the packaging — return it as is.
real-situation; crucial for returns/exchanges, in negative -지 말다 form
nuance: 뜯다 means to tear, rip, or peel something open by pulling it apart — a snack bag, a delivery box, an envelope, a protective film — usually destructively and irreversibly. The contrast learners must hold is with 풀다 (to untie/undo, reversibly): you 풀어 a ribbon, a knot, or shoelaces and could re-tie them, but you 뜯어 sealed tape or a glued flap and there's no going back. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The headline pitfall is conjugation: because it ends in ㄷ, English speakers assume the ㄷ-irregular and write 뜰어요 — but 뜯다 is REGULAR (like 받다, 묻다 'bury', 믿다), so the ㄷ stays put: 뜯어요, 뜯었어요. Only true ㄷ-irregulars like 듣다 → 들어요 and 걷다 → 걸어요 change ㄷ to ㄹ.

Using 풀다 to open sealed packaging — 풀다 is for undoing something tied or knotted (리본을 풀다). Sealed tape, bags, and boxes are 뜯다.
Saying 열다 ('open') for a snack bag or a vacuum-sealed packet — 열다 fits doors and lids; tearing into sealed packaging is 봉지를 뜯다.

usage: 에 marks where it hangs; the prototypical 'hang up a coat' scene
a separate everyday sense: you 'hang/place' a call — 전화 걸게 'I'll call you'
to put a lock on / latch
fastening a lock or latch: 문에 자물쇠를 걸다
걸다 + 두다 = hang it and leave it there (수건을 걸어 두다)
examples: 여기 걸어.
Hang it here.
casual; 걸 + 어 = 걸어요 in the present, the ㄹ survives before a vowel
벽에 액자 좀 걸어 줄 수 있어요?
Can you hang the picture frame on the wall?
everyday moving-in/decorating request
나가기 전에 문 잠그고 자물쇠 걸었는지 꼭 확인하세요.
Before leaving, make sure you locked the door and latched the lock.
real-situation; 걸다 = fasten a lock, and note the formal 겁니다 drops the ㄹ
nuance: 걸다 means to hang something on a hook, hanger, wall, or rail — a coat, a towel, a picture frame — and it stretches to latching a lock (자물쇠를 걸다) and, in a major separate sense, placing a phone call (전화를 걸다 'to call'). To take a hung thing back down you 내리다 or 떼다. The grammar story is the heart of this word: 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular, so the stem ㄹ DROPS before endings starting with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ — giving the formal 겁니다 (not 걸읍니다) and the future 걸 거예요 — yet the ㄹ stays before a vowel, keeping the present 걸어요. There's no 한자; it's native. Pitfall: English speakers force the formal as 걸읍니다 by analogy with regular verbs, and they may miss that 'make a call' in Korean is literally 'hang a call,' 전화를 걸다.

Using 걸다 to mean 'take down' — 걸다 only hangs up; to remove a hung item you need 내리다 (take down) or 떼다 (detach).

usage: piling things tall — 박스를 높이 쌓다 'stack boxes high'
figurative: accumulate career/experience over time (경험을 쌓다 likewise)
the passive partner, just as common: 눈이 쌓이다 'snow piles up,' 스트레스가 쌓이다
figurative; relationships and trust are 'stacked up' over time
examples: 여기 쌓아.
Stack them here.
casual; 쌓 + 아 = 쌓아요, the ㅎ stays silent but written
설거지통에 그릇을 너무 높이 쌓지 마.
Don't stack the dishes too high in the sink.
everyday home line; 쌓다 + 높이 = pile up tall, in negative -지 마
이 일을 하면서 경력을 차근차근 쌓고 있어요.
I'm steadily building up my career through this job.
real-situation figurative; 경력을 쌓다 = accumulate career, 차근차근 = step by step
nuance: 쌓다 means to stack or pile things on top of one another — dishes, boxes, books — and it has a rich figurative life for accumulating things that build up over time: 경력을 쌓다 (build a career), 경험을 쌓다, 신뢰를 쌓다, 스트레스가 쌓이다. Its passive partner 쌓이다 ('be piled up / accumulate,' as in 눈이 쌓이다 'snow accumulates') is just as frequent in daily speech, so learn the active/passive pair together. Don't confuse it with 모으다 (to gather/collect scattered things into one place, like 돈을 모으다 'save money' or 우표를 모으다 'collect stamps'); 쌓다 is specifically layering up, 모으다 is bringing together. It's a native verb, no 한자, and although it ends in ㅎ it conjugates regularly: 쌓 + 아요 = 쌓아요. Pitfall: the ㅎ is silent but must be written — 쌓아요, not 싸아요.

mistakes: Dropping the ㅎ in writing — it is silent in speech but the spelling keeps it: 쌓아요, 쌓았어요, never 싸아요.

usage: 꽉 (tightly) is the habitual partner; said on buses/subways about the strap
literally 'grip a fist' — close the whole hand
closing the fist around a bar, strap, or handle for safety
to have firmly in hand — also figurative: 정보를 손에 쥐다 'hold information'
examples: 손 꽉 쥐어.
Grip my hand tight.
casual; 쥐 + 어 = 쥐어요 (often spoken 줘요), and 꽉 = tightly
펜을 너무 세게 쥐면 손이 아파요.
If you grip the pen too hard, your hand hurts.
everyday; 쥐다 = clench the fist around something, with conditional -면
지하철 흔들리니까 손잡이 잘 쥐고 계세요.
The subway's shaky, so keep a good grip on the strap.
real-situation safety reminder; honorific 계시다 + 쥐고 = keep gripping
nuance: 쥐다 means to grip or clench — to close your hand firmly around something like a handle, a pen, or a strap, and it is the verb behind 주먹을 쥐다 'to make a fist.' What sets it apart from its neighbors is the whole-hand squeezing grasp: 집다 picks a small thing up with the fingertips (you 집어 a coin), and 잡다 is the broad 'catch/hold/grab' (you 잡아 a taxi, a hand, or a chance), but 쥐다 specifically clenches the fist tight around an object. Figuratively it implies holding power or information firmly — 주도권을 쥐다 'hold the initiative.' It's a native verb, no 한자, and as a ㅟ-stem it conjugates 쥐 + 어 = 쥐어요 (colloquially heard as 줘요), with the formal 쥡니다. Pitfall: English speakers blur 쥐다 and 집다, but you 쥐어 a railing and 집어 a single fry.
